message.content:
**About 2 hours 11 minutes: 7,875 seconds** after the connection last carried data, using stock kernel defaults.

The figure comes from three system-wide sysctls under `net.ipv4` (also visible in `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/`):

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| `tcp_keepalive_time` | 7200 s | Idle time before the first keepalive probe is sent |
| `tcp_keepalive_intvl` | 75 s | Gap between successive unanswered probes |
| `tcp_keepalive_probes` | 9 | Unanswered probes before the connection is aborted |

The sequence is as follows. The socket sits idle for 7,200 seconds, then the kernel sends the first probe. The dead peer never answers, so the kernel sends further probes every 75 seconds. After the ninth probe has also gone unanswered for a full interval, the kernel aborts the connection and the application sees ETIMEDOUT.

```
7200 + 9 × 75 = 7875 seconds  (2 h 11 min 15 s)
```

The ninth probe itself goes out at 7,800 seconds. Linux waits one more interval after the last probe before giving up, so 7,800 is off by one interval and 7,875 is the correct total.

Two caveats affect how this maps onto wall-clock time:

- **The clock starts at the last activity, not at the power loss.** If the connection was already idle when the peer died, part of the 7,200-second idle period had already elapsed, so the connection is declared dead less than 7,875 seconds after the outage.
- **Keepalive only governs a fully idle connection.** If unacknowledged data were in flight, the retransmission timer and `tcp_retries2` would apply instead, giving a shorter timeout of roughly 15 to 30 minutes. The question specifies no application traffic, so keepalive is the only mechanism here.

A powered-off peer simply goes silent, so no RST or ICMP error arrives to shortcut the process, and the full keepalive timeout applies. Distributions occasionally ship different sysctl defaults, so check the actual values on the host if precise timing matters.

Roughly 2 hours and 11 minutes, which is 7875 seconds, on stock kernel defaults.

The figure comes from three sysctls in `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/`:

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| tcp_keepalive_time | 7200 s | Idle time before the first probe is sent |
| tcp_keepalive_intvl | 75 s | Gap between successive unanswered probes |
| tcp_keepalive_probes | 9 | Unanswered probes before the connection is declared dead |

The connection is idle, so after 7200 seconds the kernel sends the first probe. The dead peer never ACKs it, so the kernel sends further probes every 75 seconds. Once 9 probes have gone unanswered, it aborts the connection with ETIMEDOUT.

The arithmetic is 7200 + 9 × 75 = 7875 seconds, about 2 h 11 m 15 s. The alternative reading, that the ninth unanswered probe fires the timeout after 7200 + 8 × 75 = 7800 seconds, is off by one interval: Linux waits `intvl` after the last probe before giving up, so 7875 is the correct total.

Two caveats matter in practice. If the peer host stays up but the process dies, or an intermediate router replies with ICMP unreachable, you get a RST or error much sooner, but a powered-off peer simply goes silent, so the full timeout applies. Also, if the application has unacknowledged data in flight when the peer disappears, retransmission logic governed by `tcp_retries2` applies instead of keepalive, giving a different timeout of about 15 to 30 minutes. The question specifies no traffic, so keepalive is the only mechanism, and 7875 seconds is the answer.

With the usual Linux defaults, the nominal timeout is **7,875 seconds—2 hours, 11 minutes, 15 seconds—since the last activity that reset the keepalive idle timer**:

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| `net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time` | 7,200 s | Idle time before sending the first probe |
| `net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_intvl` | 75 s | Interval between unanswered probes |
| `net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_probes` | 9 | Number of unanswered probes before giving up |

The calculation is **7,200 + (9 × 75) = 7,875 seconds**. The ninth probe is sent at 7,800 seconds; the kernel gives up one interval later if no response arrives.

That is **not necessarily 7,875 seconds after the peer loses power**: the connection may already have been idle, so some of the timer may have elapsed. Actual timing also depends on kernel scheduling, and system-wide sysctl settings can differ from these defaults even without per-socket overrides.

On a stock Linux system, the kernel will declare the connection dead after exactly **7,875 seconds** (which is **2 hours, 11 minutes, and 15 seconds**).

This figure comes from the standard default values of three `sysctl` kernel parameters (located under `net.ipv4`):

1. **`tcp_keepalive_time` (default: 7200)** 
   The initial period of idle time (in seconds) the connection must be completely quiet before the kernel sends the very first keepalive probe.
2. **`tcp_keepalive_intvl` (default: 75)** 
   The time interval (in seconds) to wait for a response before sending the next probe.
3. **`tcp_keepalive_probes` (default: 9)** 
   The maximum number of consecutive unacknowledged probes the kernel will send before giving up and dropping the connection.

**The calculation:**
Because there is no application traffic and the peer is dead, the socket sits idle. 
* The kernel waits **7,200 seconds** and then sends the 1st keepalive probe. 
* Receiving no TCP ACK (because the peer lost power), it then sends **9** unacknowledged probes, waiting **75 seconds** after each one.
* Total time = `tcp_keepalive_time` + (`tcp_keepalive_intvl` * `tcp_keepalive_probes`)
* Total time = 7200 + (75 * 9) = 7200 + 675 = **7,875 seconds**.

members.answer:
**Answer**

On a stock Linux kernel (no per‑socket overrides), the keep‑alive timer that finally declares a TCP connection dead is built from three system‑wide parameters found under */proc/sys/net/ipv4*:

| Parameter (kernel name) | Meaning | Default value (Linux) |
|--------------------------|---------|-----------------------|
| `tcp_keepalive_time`     | How long the socket must be idle before the **first** keep‑alive probe is sent. | **7200 s** (2 hours) |
| `tcp_keepalive_intvl`    | Interval between successive keep‑alive probes after the first one. | **75 s** |
| `tcp_keepalive_probes`   | Number of unanswered probes after which the kernel gives up and marks the connection dead. | **9** probes |

The total time the kernel will wait before declaring the connection dead is therefore  

\[
\text{total} = \text{tcp\_keepalive\_time} + (\text{tcp\_keepalive\_probes} \times \text{tcp\_keepalive\_intvl})
\]

Plugging in the defaults:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{total} &= 7200\;\text{s} + (9 \times 75\;\text{s}) \\
             &= 7200\;\text{s} + 675\;\text{s} \\
             &= 7875\;\text{s}
\end{aligned}
\]

**7875 seconds ≈ 2 hours 11 minutes 15 seconds**

So, after the peer goes silent (e.g., loses power) and there is no other traffic, the Linux kernel will wait **about 2 h 11 min** before it declares the TCP connection dead, using the three parameters shown above.

*If any of these sysctl values have been changed on the host, the deadline will be correspondingly different.*
